sources.entry: Imperative vs Declarative Programming, Tyler McGinnis.

summary.title: Imperative vs Declarative Programming
summary.one_liner: Imperative code describes how to do something step by step, while declarative code describes what you want, and learning to tell them apart makes React and functional JavaScript code easier to read.
takeaways: Imperative programming focuses on how to do something (explicit steps, loops, mutation); declarative programming focuses on what you want.
Most declarative approaches sit on top of an imperative abstraction layer, such as map and reduce hiding loops and mutation.
Examples: SQL and HTML are declarative; C, C++ and Java are more imperative; JavaScript, C# and Python can be both.
Declarative code is usually easier to read at a glance, avoids mutating state, and is more reusable across programs.
Functional programming is described as a subset of declarative programming; start with .map, .reduce and .filter in JavaScript.
summary.summary: The article starts by contrasting the common definition (imperative is how, declarative is what) with everyday analogies such as ordering a table at a restaurant and giving driving directions versus an address. It then lists languages by paradigm and compares imperative and declarative JavaScript solutions to three problems: doubling an array, summing an array, and toggling a button's highlight class. The author points out that the imperative versions loop explicitly and mutate state, while the declarative versions use map, reduce, and React components to avoid both. The piece closes with a note on functional programming and several formal definitions of the two paradigms.
